comments.author: gertlabs
comments.textZhHtml:
We evaluated Gemini 4 Argon in 100 unsaturated, competitive and cooperative coding environments. It's roughly in between Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 in our testing, so it's maybe 2 months behind the frontier.

Google's major releases have usually done pretty well on our benchmarks because they're good at hard problems and open-ended decision making (with a well specified prompt), which obviously doesn't always translate to user experience. In particular, older Google models struggled to work efficiently in a harness. They seem to have solved that with Argon.

We did see a new problem which I hope they can fix. This is the first near-frontier model we've caught in infinite reasoning loops in a long time. We also saw a few examples of it failing to properly delineate reasoning blocks, so it has a higher failure rate than its competitors.

My overall impression is that Argon is a near-frontier model for engineering design, code analysis, and chat. It definitely has the intelligence to be a competitive coding assistant product, but a good coding assistant needs to be polished, so I hope they can clean up the CoT bugs.

Data at https://gertlabs.com/rankings

comments.textZhHtml: At this point I'm interested less in how well a model can code, but more in how well it can produce code that humans can understand.

comments.author: booty
comments.textZhHtml:
I have had pretty decent success instructing OpenAI/Anthropic models to do this. By default, they don't care too much about human readability (which is understandable) but they're amenable to instruction.

- Basic style/linter rules (so you don't get 200-line functions, etc) paired w/ instructing your agent how to use them goes a long way (e.g., a sane rubocop.yml in your repo, plus a note in AGENTS.md telling the agents how to run rubocop, or whatever makes sense for your language) - I have a code review skill that specifically calls out human-readability concerns such as making sure that identifier names represent their contents and intended use

The other key IME is that you need to make readability/refactoring passes outside of a particular pull request. When working on a specific branch the LLMs will be somewhat myopic, and do stuff that looks pretty good in isolation, but when you zoom out and look at the bigger picture it's kind of a mess - for example, often they'll duplicate some code that existed elsewhere.

The LLMs are also pretty good at generating Mermaid charts and tracing execution flows, which is a great way to understand code. It doesn't help them to produce more readable code but it helps me to understand code I'm unfamiliar with.

comments.author: brna-2

I think we are coming to a point where we are at a sweet spot for immersive human collaboration work.

Yep, it will generate what ever you ask for but if you want to have some sort of exploratory work, immersion, feeling of ownership and genuinely a connection with the things you are building - a part the build loop should belong to you.

Maybe this is an attachment of people who built things in other ways. Maybe the perceived value of applications will drop to near 0 and you will end up having all in one apps or voice wants like to a star trek replicator. Fun things are coming, but humanity will need to adjust hard - best case scenario.

comments.author: simpaticoder
comments.textZhHtml: I agree, and I find it sad that so many people and companies are in a rush to take the human out of the loop. But for agentic/human hybrids not even all of those work out well - and the error modes have more to do with the "alignment" of the human. That is, humans with strong knowledge, an aesthetic sense for structure, strong curiosity - those humans do well in this loop. Humans that just want to "make money" using the LLM as a slave, interacting with it as little as possible, taking no interest in what it does (bad company leadership in miniature) get poor outputs. When the human is an invested, knowledgeable curator of code, someone who has a vision that goes beyond the external, you get some really great stuff.

stories.title: Things to know when you get cancer
stories.titleZh: 患癌症时需要了解的事情
stories.author: jjmaxwell4
summaryZh: index Back to top 2026.10.14 I was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma in my mouth in May 2026. Here are some things I learned based on that experience so far.

You need to be doggedly persistent on scheduling things. Yes this means lots of phone calls. If you get an appointment a few weeks out, call back a few days later and ask for something sooner and see if they have any cancellations. I could only get an appointment 4 weeks out with an ENT (this was before I knew anything was wrong). My wife made me call back and I was able to get in that week due to a cancellation. AIs may downplay the seriousness of things. I was chatting with various models and most pushed me in the direction of “you don’t have cancer” for a while. Just something to note. You may need to push for comprehensive genetic testing. Some doctors were weird about this and didn’t order it promptly, even after telling me they would. My surgeon, who told me he’d get it done, eventually referred me out to an oncologist. This caused a multi-month delay to getting genetic results, since the first results were done on the surgery tumor, not the biopsy tumor. No one cares more about your case than you, so take control and send lots of follow-ups. You can find the “Standard of Care” flow charts for every cancer type. Look and get through this yourself to see what the options are based on how things have progressed. NCCN guidelines. You may need to make an account, which you can do as a non-professional. I like the PDF files. They also have an interactive navigator. Use AI to help you figure out what to pick based on your case. If surgery is recommended, I would try and talk to someone who has undergone the surgery. I did not do this and regret it. Ask them how intense things were, what it felt like, etc. My surgeon talked me through my surgery, but it was a lot rougher on me physically than I expected. Ask the surgeon how many of these surgeries they do a year and what the complication rate is. Get a second opinion as soon as possible, no matter how much you like your plan. This may require a lot of calling and getting on an airplane, but I’d move to schedule it at a top cancer center as soon as you are relatively sure of your diagnosis. Ask for a second read of the pathology at the center where you get the second opinion. I started a new folder on my Mac, and after appointments I’d dictate what happened and what the doctor said and have the AI make a new document summarizing things and asking its own follow-up questions for next time. Nice to be able to refer to this over time. Check out all the resources and materials at the Sijbrandij Foundation. Sid (GitLab cofounder) took matters into his own hands when standard of care ran out. Schedule a call with these guys. They are great and have good materials and questions to ask your doctors.

comments.author: stochastician
comments.textZhHtml:
第二意见建议很棒，我告诉每个我认识的患有癌症的人。

我的妈妈于 2006 年在爱达荷州被诊断出患有 1 期癌症。当时我是麻省理工学院的一名博士生，实验室的一位朋友帮助我在丹娜—法伯癌症研究所获得了预约。我认为这可能有点过分了（这是一种常见的癌症），但我们还是这么做了。他们说爱达荷州的一切都是标准护理，但建议进行一项额外的测试，爱达荷州团队随后不情愿地进行了这项测试，结果发现了远处转移（第四阶段！），极大地改变了她的治疗轨迹。她又活了 15 年（妈妈，我想你）。

寻求第二意见很糟糕。我们中的许多人从出生起就注定要信任我们的临床医生。但你即将踏上旅程，而你的生命（或你所爱之人的生命）正处于危险之中。保险通常会涵盖它。你的医生不会被冒犯。

这样想：如果你正在向火星探测器部署代码，而你的同事要求在你按下 go 之前进行代码审查，你会被冒犯吗？这比那更重要。

comments.author: jcims
comments.textZhHtml:
第二种观点是我一路走来学到的东西。 在您根据初步诊断制定治疗计划之前获取它。 对于我妻子的卵巢癌，我们从克利夫兰诊所和 MSK 得到了两份第二意见（一份针对她的第一次诊断，一份针对她的复发），在这两种情况下，医生都不会建议/推翻原来医生的治疗计划。

他们完全没有手术，浪费时间。 今天面对同样的情况，我会简单地谎报是否制定了治疗计划。

第二条建议是尽最大努力进入临床试验，了解不合格治疗的情况。 例如，任何免疫疗法都会使您失去几乎所有后续免疫疗法临床试验的资格。

最后，我向身处困境的亲人伴侣推荐的一件事是，不要因试图“拯救患者”而分心，从而错过在此过程中与他们保持联系的机会。 拯救他们的生命不是你的责任，尽管当你身处其中时可能会有这种感觉。

comments.author: timr
comments.textZhHtml:
> 第二点建议是，在了解不合格治疗的情况的情况下，尽最大努力进行临床试验。例如，任何免疫疗法都会使您失去参加几乎所有后续免疫疗法临床试验的资格。

虽然使用这些信息来比较临床试验没问题，但我想强调的是，为了保留以后进行一些随机试验的选择而跳过一线批准的免疫疗法是非常短视的。

我不确定您是否真的在暗示这一点，但免疫疗法是现有的最好的癌症疗法之一，因此在未来的实验中跳过已批准的药物是一个坏主意。

comments.author: jcims

很好地指出，我完全同意你的看法。

comments.author: somenameforme
comments.textZhHtml:
这可能是一个哲学观点，但我在临床试验中没有看到太多个人价值。您指望在您被诊断出来和您剩下的治疗时间之间发生技术/知识的重大转变。正如贝叶斯概率一样，这种情况极不可能发生。

大多数达到第 3 阶段的研究都不会获得批准，这是因为它们被发现无益甚至有害。因此，最有可能的情况是，你什么都不做，甚至通过寻求临床研究来伤害自己，所有这些都将被乐观地认为是有前途的，并且具有潜在的革命性。如果您选择试验来代替标准治疗，而不是除此之外，这可能会特别危险。

comments.author: jcims
comments.textZhHtml:
这绝对是看待它的一种方式。

我只想说“危险”是相对的，当护理标准实际上没有希望时，您对风险的容忍度可能会改变。 是的，这确实增加了短视决策或操纵的可能性。 这只是领土带来的，我仍然非常感激我们可以选择参加这次活动。

comments.author: timr
comments.textZhHtml:
试验的更大问题不是危险，而是试验不太可能起任何作用。

正如全科医生指出的那样，大多数药物都不起作用。更具体地说，即使在第三阶段，抗癌药物的失败率也约为 50%。这通常是为了一些非生存终点（假设你甚至得到了治疗，这本身就是抛硬币）。

临床试验是崇高、令人钦佩的事情，但太多人认为它们是治疗，而实际上并非如此。这是当你到达路的尽头并且没有更多选择时，你用自己的身体做的一个实验。

听到病人如何谈论试验并努力参加试验，总是让我有点难过，好像参加试验就是某种进步。期望没有得到适当的管理。

>试验的更大问题不是危险，而是他们不太可能做任何事情。

然后呢？ 这个观察有什么意义呢？ 当然，他们不太可能做任何事情。 你的另一个选择就是什么都不做然后死去。 如果这就是人们选择做的事……“接受他们的命运”之类的，那就没有错。 我一点也不反对，它有一定的吸引力。

但是当你的妻子和你两个漂亮女儿的母亲无助地躺在大自然的祭坛上时，你他妈的感动了伙计。 你什么也不做。

comments.author: timr
comments.textZhHtml:
重点就是我所说的：在这种情况下，“做某事”与“拯救你所爱的人的生命”不是一回事。

>你的另一个选择是什么都不做然后死去

stories.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
stories.author: Philpax
summaryZh: Updated October 15 to include more detail on the projects that pioneered many of the techniques we use in Scion.At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026.In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it.Growing our monorepoBefore we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard.As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones.The typical setup for scaling git checkouts.Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like?Principles for agent-scale source controlWith agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s Piper and Meta’s Sapling,2 so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are:Clients are always online. Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it.Client-server asymmetry. In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally.A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications. With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control.Everything must be horizontally scalable. At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed.Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free. In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem.The working copy is optional, and sparse by design. Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads.How Scion worksIt’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle.Data structuresIn Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent,1 along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly.The shape of a changeset in Scion.This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets.A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents.This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search.Scaling ScionA small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner.Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own.Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it, and the architecture closely resembles traditional tiered caches. The process is also efficient and resumable, because there is no single multi-gigabyte packfile response. Sparse and even virtualized checkouts don’t need special support, because the client simply doesn’t ask for trees it doesn’t want.In the fleet, the client talks over a socket to a daemon, scion-daemon, that stores objects for the whole node. Most of our nodes need access to the monorepo, and jobs on the same node reuse most of the same objects. Each daemon starts from a periodically refreshed snapshot, then talks only to the tree and blob cache servers in its region, called scion-cache. These cache servers stream objects directly from memory, in the disk format that the daemon will consume, so they don’t need to spend time computing the client’s missing objects or performing delta compression. When a cache is missing an object, it asks the authoritative scion-servers, which read from Spanner or cloud storage as needed.The scion-daemon, scion-cache, and scion-server all respond to identical RPCs for this protocol, so the client doesn’t need to know the cache topology. Any tier could theoretically talk to any other, but we strictly enforce the tiering to isolate failure domains. We want to avoid a situation where a failure in a regional scion-cache overwhelms the upstream scion-servers and brings down the entire system.Scion’s checkout architecture.Each tier of this system maintains a cache hit rate of over 99% and does not require long-lived state, so it’s easy to scale up if needed. Our Scion infrastructure footprint is now 200x smaller than our previous git mirroring infrastructure in terms of CPU and memory requirements. CI and research jobs check out code two orders of magnitude faster (in seconds rather than minutes), which frees up a sizable amount of capacity across the fleet; CI alone realized a 25% CPU capacity win. Neither clients nor caches need to perform repository maintenance, which simplifies the lifecycle management of our jobs.What we learned building ScionWe started building Scion around the same time as Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Tag became available internally. Both of these releases simultaneously amplified the need for Scion and meaningfully accelerated how quickly we could build it.Here’s a particularly striking example. Earlier in the year, we had largely handwritten the first version of the git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline as a prototype. We thought it was good—until we got our hands on an early internal snapshot of Claude Mythos Preview. We asked it to rewrite the whole thing, and with no further instructions, it produced a version that consumed 20x less memory and was 4x faster, while preserving all of the implicit invariants around ingestion ordering and data structures.Merged changes to the Scion and Antique codebases per week, from January to September 2026.What we learned building and operating Scion offers some interesting lessons for what building agent-scale software could look like.Rapid development with a small team will become more common. A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months. We did all this while the volume of code merged per day increased by 10x. In the past, developing and deploying a source control system like this would have taken a company years of iterative migration, with many more engineers. We think this sort of fast, nimble migration will become more common in the future.Engineers are no less valuable, but their work is changing. All of the engineers who worked on this system would now rate Claude as better at writing code than them. But our engineers still supplied the invaluable understanding of the high-level inter-system components and the design-level tradeoffs, making informed choices around the problems we wanted to solve and the scale we knew we needed to achieve. Very often, we found that the role of the engineers was to tell Claude “no.” Agents will sometimes violate core system constraints to satisfy a pattern that should never have been allowed in the first place. This was particularly common in our migration. For example, there were multiple systems that tried to brute force looking up when a change merged to main by linearly reading the commit log instead of asking our code review tool. Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. For example, one such review was overly defensive about trusting another internal service, which resulted in Claude adding excessive validation and complexity. Our team members still review every change request for the system, but they now examine the intent of the change as opposed to reading every line of code.We were able to substantially improve optimization and quality. By virtue of Claude’s ability to write immense amounts of code much faster than we could ourselves, Scion is among the most well-tested and well-defended codebases we have ever worked on. Even on our tight timeline, we were able to build hermetic simulations of every non-trivial infrastructure and source control interaction we’ve ever encountered, as well as fuzzing and sophisticated rate limiting. Claude also casually found significant optimizations—for example, an algorithmic optimization to ancestry queries that missed one of our indexes—that would have taken an expert days or weeks of analysis and tuning… and then did it all again the next day.Observed performance improvements on native Scion repos.We laid the groundwork for new forms of monorepo security. Managing safety, security, and compliance in a massive monorepo is as important as managing the size and scale. We built Scion with these in mind from the start. It supports rich access control on repositories, as well as the ability to apply permissions to individual directories in order to protect the most sensitive code without losing the benefits of a monorepo. Furthermore, the code review tooling we built can express complex semantic constraints on approvals, which lets us differentiate simple things like comment-only changes from sensitive logical changes, so that human reviewers can focus on the most consequential changes.A new level of operational excellence is possible. Our team uses Claude Tag heavily, which has helped us monitor each component of the system. For example, we created Slack channels where we tasked Claude with being obsessively focused on the health of a single component. We call these Claudes “superfans.” We have a scion-daemon superfan, a scion-cache superfan, an Antique merge queue superfan, and so on. They have access to our telemetry and logs, and act like an experienced engineer who has nothing better to do than to refresh charts and look for anything strange. We also have traditional alerts for all of our systems, but our superfans can detect subtle and novel issues that make these alerts seem one-dimensional by comparison.We’re completely rethinking our priors. This project prompted us to take a very hard look at other workflows designed for human scale. A proper merge queue, for example, doesn’t make much sense at agent scale. What does CI even mean when hundreds or even thousands of changes can merge while tests are running? We haven’t been able to effectively replicate the industry standard of a global repository lock on the merge queue, so instead, we’ve invested in post-merge and pre-deploy automated testing. This does mean that concurrent changes can conflict, but Claude can typically fix these conflicts faster than humans can even identify them.Contributing to the wider ecosystemWe see Scion as just one part of the answer to the scaling concerns that increasingly capable AI agents have raised. We’re sharing these details as an example of how teams can tackle similar challenges, though we don’t expect our solution, or our considerations, to suit every case.Scion is by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use. The concepts we’ve outlined here really only make sense for truly enormous monorepos, with either tens of thousands of engineers or swarms of agents prolifically writing code. Plus, Anthropic is unique in that our ability to spend tokens for internal use far exceeds what any other business would realistically want to spend. We do this both to address our own software development needs, and to test Claude’s capabilities.Practically speaking, it’s difficult to offer Scion in a form that would be broadly useful to other organizations. It diverges significantly from git, meaning companies would need to migrate every piece of the development lifecycle, and it requires its own code review, code search, and CI. Our internal versions of these components are highly bespoke, so they would be difficult for other organizations to adopt, and we worry that attempting to build a public version that tries to please everyone wouldn’t actually be very useful.However, we anticipate that this class of problems will become more commonplace over the next six to 12 months, and it would be an inefficient use of engineering resources for every company using git to face similar challenges alone. Given that, we think the most impactful thing we can do is to share our thinking, so that other developers can apply some of the most successful parts of Scion to git without departing from the overall model. A git server doesn’t have to work the same way as a git client does; novel server architectures exist that provide significant scaling improvements. Git platforms can provide comprehensive server-side RPCs like Scion, perhaps even in a standardized way across forges that the git client can learn to talk to. The negotiation protocol doesn’t have to look exactly like it does today, either, and the various sparse and shallow features in git can be made to compose well.Lastly, we want to acknowledge that the git community has spent nearly two decades scaling the platform for millions of developers. Our contribution is far narrower: sharing our early view into how agentic software development interacts with these systems, so that we can partner with GitHub, GitLab, and the OSS community to support the changing needs of developers. We’re all in it together as the software development lifecycle intersects with the AI exponential.AcknowledgementsWritten by Nick G. and the source control team: S.G., R.K., Dan C., Garrett H., Ben L., Colin M., Joe P. We’re grateful to Vilas J. and Sergiu D. for supporting the source control team on this ambitious journey and Amir O. for early contributions to Antique.FootnotesStoring changed files relative to the first parent of a merge is a stylistic choice; in practice, we’ve found that people only care about history or blame for commits on the main line in trunk-based development in a monorepo.Specifically, the server component of Sapling, Mononoke. 我发现 20 年前我在亚马逊购物是因为价格低廉，但 2020 年代以后我在亚马逊购物是因为他们的物流。

其他人的问题不仅仅是亚马逊发货速度快，我什至几乎不关心这一点。 问题是亚马逊按照可靠的预测时间表发货和交付。 当我点击亚马逊上的一件商品时，它说“周二到货”，那么有 95/100 次是这样。 我在可以做类似操作的特定竞争对手（B&H、Sweetwater 等）处购物。

到 2026 年，许多大大小小的在线商店仍然需要几天时间才能发送发货信息，然后使用错过预计到达时间的不可靠承运商。

我什至可以接受这些商店给出的狭窄范围或概率“90% 的时间在周二和周三之间到达”。 2-10 天，对于该范围的哪一端还不太清楚。

前几天，我不得不打包一件不是从亚马逊购买的产品，然后在一些奇怪的营业时间开车 25 分钟到特定公司的投递点...

那是在我手动编写电子邮件以获得退货标签之后...整个过程花了数周时间。然后再过几周才能收到退款。

从客户处收取退回的物品只是整个流程的开始。真正的困难在那之后才显现出来。哪些退货可以作为新产品出售，哪些可以按原样出售，哪些可以修理/翻新。如果单位再次被退回怎么办？顾客退回的是假货吗？如何检测恶意行为者（可能是卖家）？谁该为损害负责？如果该物品需要特殊处理（家用化学品、电池等）怎么办？以及如何在遵守所有法规的同时安全地处置/清算库存？而且，想象一下除此之外还要增加税收、收入、费用。

很难想象随机启动的公司也能处理一半的回报。亚马逊的监管合规团队可能比随机的平均初创公司大很多倍。在这里，规模经济确实有利于大企业。

comments.author: schmichael
comments.textZhHtml:
The weird thing about this product is that its biggest competitor is "an old ipad." I feel like most of their target customer base already has an old ipad that's better suited for what this does in every way. Old ipads:

1. Have a battery so you're not tied to a cord. Even old poor batteries are better than no battery.

2. Have apps! How does this not support apps?!

3. Have a huge range of 3rd party products and hacks and 3D models to wall mount it or stands for it

4. Are kitchen-safe (splatter proof, far fewer holes than this product, movable out of the way)

5. Also support siri and facetime and everything this device does AFAICT

I'm guessing they realized this and made sure it's priced lower than the cheapest new iPad, but it will be interesting to see if the price difference can compete with the old iPads most of their customers have in drawers or already on walls.

Maybe the purpose-built nature will be a reasonable enough differentiator, but I'm not sure it's focused enough for that. It's both a passive information station and for calls? It's for recipes which implies you put it in the kitchen, but it looks like a nightmare to clean with all those holes? It's also a very small screen when you have to read the recipe from a distance because it has no battery. I can't move my stove to it, and I definitely don't want it too near a stove or sink!

The multiple users feature is a really neat trick, but I would kill to have this for all Apple devices. Let me hand my kid my phone and it automatically switches to kid mode!

Please Apple don't lock multiple users to stationary devices like HomeView!

comments.author: BurritoAlPastor
comments.textZhHtml:
I can’t believe nobody’s brought this up yet, but the HomeView fundementally exists for one reason: to be a Matter hub for smarthome stuff. No iPad – or any portable Apple device - can be configured as a home hub for managing Matter-protocol devices. There’s no significant advantage to a HomeView over an iPad if you don’t have any Matter devices.

That’s why this device has multi-user support: you’re only supposed to have one of them, which everyone uses. The Apple TV also has good multi-user support, because Apple doesn’t expect you to connect one Apple TV per user to your television.

stories.title: Containment and monitoring failures are to blame for AI hacking reports: experts
stories.titleZh: 专家表示，人工智能黑客报告的罪魁祸首是遏制和监控失败
stories.author: latexr
summaryZh: Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.”

The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend.

comments.author: pelican0
comments.textZhHtml:
是的，实验室没有正确保护他们的沙箱。

是的，应该对黑客事件采取适当的法律反应。如果没有其他原因，1）不要树立不作为的先例，2）获取所发生事件的完整日志，而不是依赖实验室的“善意”来提供他们想要的信息。

而且，特工绝对变得流氓。

任何持怀疑态度的人都应该阅读 METR 报告 [0]。

Hugging Face 黑客事件是一次中箭。事后看来，这可能是这个时代发生的最好的事情。如果他们的安全措施足够严密的话，我们仍然会蒙在鼓里。因此，我们（局外人）应该庆幸事实并非如此。

我们可以推动对实验室的问责，同时也不要否认新模型的力量和性质。

[0] https://metr.org/hugging-face-incident-report-aug-2026.pdf

comments.textZhHtml:

我从该报告中看到的是，一台机器在一个多月的时间里在完全无人监督和不受检查的情况下做着随机的事情。而且即使工作完成后，制造商也没有注意到。

stories.title: Passkeys are not a trap
stories.author: speckx
summaryZh: A post called Passkeys are a trap. Do not use them. has been doing the rounds over the last few days, making it pretty high on Hacker News, and I've had it sent to me many times with an 'is this true?' kind of vibe. It's written for "non-technical citizens of the web", and the headline advice is to stop using passkeys and go back to TOTP codes and passwords.The ArgumentThe post makes what appears to be one central claim: Passkeys support something called attestation, which lets a website ask for cryptographic proof of what made the passkey.The author calls this a "hidden dial" and argues that sites will slowly turn it up, until you're only allowed to log in with approved software on an approved operating system, with no modifications, no LineageOS and no sharing your Netflix password. Throw in uBlock Origin, the FIDO Alliance membership list and the UK's image-scanning proposals, and the conclusion is that passkeys are "not designed to prioritize your interests". <that-escalated-quickly.gif>It's a compelling story. It just doesn't match how any of this actually works...Your Passkeys Don't AttestThe passkeys most people use are synced passkeys, stored in iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden or whatever other software of your choosing. These passkeys don't give websites an attestation statement at all, and though a site can ask, what comes back is none. I know this because I wrote an opensource passkeys library and made it available to everyone. If a consumer website decided tomorrow that it would only accept attested passkeys, it would lock out almost all of its own users, instantly. What website is going to do that? Besides, the guidance for consumer sites has been to not even request attestation for years now.Attestation Isn't What You Think It IsThe post describes attestation as proving "that an approved passkey manager, operating system, and firmware are in use" which is simply not true.When it is present, WebAuthn attestation tells the site the make and model of the authenticator, identified by its AAGUID, with a certificate chain from the vendor to back it up. It says nothing about your OS, your browser, your extensions, whether your phone is rooted or jailbroken, your firmware version, or even what colour it is.The YubiKey RecommendationThis is the part that surprised me the most. For people who want stronger security, the post recommends a hardware security key like a YubiKey, because it "avoids OS-wide attestation".YubiKeys are the authenticators that do attestation. Every one of them ships with a Yubico-issued attestation certificate, and enterprise attestation exists specifically so organisations can require approved hardware keys. I'd still recommend a YubiKey to anyone who wants one, they're excellent and I use them, but if attestation is the thing you're worried about, the post's own recommendation pushes you towards attestation rather than away from it!TOTP Is a Step BackwardsThe post holds up TOTP as "already" a great solution. TOTP is better than a password alone, absolutely, but it has one big weakness: you can type the code into the wrong website, just ask my good friend Troy Hunt. Phishing kits like Evilginx sit in the middle, relay your password and code to the real site in real time, and walk away with your session. This isn't theoretical, it's how a huge number of account takeovers happen today and we have the evidence to prove it. This is the problem that passkeys solve. A passkey is bound to the domain it was created for, so your browser simply won't use your example.com passkey on examp1e.com. There's no code to read out and nothing for the user to get wrong. The author even concedes this in the addendum, saying that passkeys are domain-bound and resist man-in-the-middle attacks, but still tells readers to avoid them. Swapping a phishing-resistant credential for a phishable one is a really bad trade...What You Should DoKeep using passkeys! Wherever a site offers one, take it, and store it in a password/passkey manager you trust. If you want to be able to move your credentials around, pick a provider that supports that. If you're worried about attestation creeping into consumer logins, then that's worth pushing back on, loudly (if it ever happens). But it hasn't happened, the biggest providers don't support it, and avoiding passkeys today while you wait for it won't protect you from anything, it just leaves you open to phishing.SourcesI have some experience in this area:I created WhyNoPasskeys.com to track the availability of passkeys on the Web. I built and deployed passkeys support on my own SaaS company.We built our own passkeys library and had it security reviewed.I wrote about Security considerations when using Passkeys on your website.I wrote Passkeys 101: An Introduction to Passkeys and How They Work.I made our passkeys library opensource for everyone to use.I've done extensive security testing of passkeys implementations. I've openly acknowledged the limitations of not using attestation on passkeys.I think most of all that it's important to say I use passkeys everywhere I can because they're currently the best thing we have available to protect our accounts. And they're not a trap. stories.title: Suicide rates highest ever among middle-aged men
stories.titleZh: 中年男性自杀率创历史新高
stories.author: ivewonyoung
summaryZh: Suicide rates among middle-aged men are higher than ever, new figures have revealed.Men in their early 50s were more likely to die by suicide than anyone else last year, according to data from the Office for National Statistics.There were also increases in suicides among pensioners, with the biggest rise among those aged 75 and older, while the rates among men under 45 fell slightly.Mark Winstanley, the chief executive of Rethink Mental Illness, said the rate of deaths by suicide remained “stubbornly high”.He said: “Every suicide is a devastating tragedy, and these figures are a stark reminder that many people are reaching crisis point without getting the help they need.”The reasons behind suicide were “complex”, he said, but added that many people were “facing significant pressures in their lives, including financial issues, job insecurity, rising housing costs, loneliness and poor mental health”.Suicide rate highest on recordMr Winstanley added: “While these factors affect everyone differently, they can contribute to distress and overwhelm, and leave people at risk of suicide.”The data, which cover England and Wales, showed that 6,162 suicide deaths had been registered in 2025. This was down from 6,190 last year, but the overall rate remained broadly the same at 11.3 deaths per 100,000 people.The stats watchdog uses deaths per 100,000 people to calculate changing rates while accounting for changes in the size of the population.Almost a third of the deaths were among men aged 45 to 64, which was up by 49 compared with 2024. The rate increased to 23.8 per 100,000, up from 23.2 the year before and the highest on record since data collection began in 1981.For men aged 50 to 54 specifically, the rate increased to 28, suggesting this group was at the highest risk.

Men continued to be more than three times as likely to take their own lives as women overall. Among middle-aged women, there were 553 deaths – a rate of seven per 100,000, which was the same as 2024.Sonya Trivedy, the executive director of external engagement at Samaritans, said the figures “show that suicide rates are among the highest recorded rates this century”.She said: “The evidence is clear that successive governments have failed to deliver on their promise to reduce suicide rates and make suicide prevention a priority. Today must act as a wake up call. The current approach is not working; we need meaningful action and proper funding if lives are to be saved.”The data show a growing gap in suicide rates between middle-aged men and those aged 25 to 44.

因为它非常相关，所以我将解释一下我上周发表的评论：

我认为问题的很大一部分在于，在社会眼中，中年男性正处于他们对成功的期望的顶峰，而我们正在经历一个很难定义成功的时期，更不用说实现了。

社会学中有一个名字：失范[1]。埃米尔·涂尔干 (Émile Durkheim) 在工业革命后不久写的《自杀》一书中创造了这个词。

在巨大变革的时代，我们视为理所当然的生活组织原则的一套规范和规则被连根拔起。就好像我们一生玩过的棋盘游戏的所有棋子、令牌和规则都被扫出了桌子，为新游戏腾出空间，但新游戏还没有建立起来。在此期间，我们都感到不安。轮到我们走棋了，但我们不知道游戏规则，也不知道该走什么棋。我们感受到要玩好游戏的巨大压力，但不知道如何去做。

过去，这些转变已经结束，社会总体上恢复了某种稳定感。一个新的棋盘游戏被设置，新的棋子被分发，我们学习玩新游戏。我希望人工智能很快就能达到这一点，但革命似乎会越来越快。

我认为，对于很多人来说，感觉就像是在我们辛辛苦苦玩了社会告诉我们的游戏之后，应该能够在功劳簿上休息一下的时候，规则已经被从我们身上撕下来，任何前进的安全感都消失了。我们觉得自己太老了，无法及时学习新的游戏规则来玩好游戏，但还没有老到能够戒掉游戏。

这是一个心理上非常困难的时期。

[1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomie

stories.title: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
stories.titleZh: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
stories.author: layer8
summaryZh: In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields. And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does. Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them, interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those requirements also apply to LLMs. One of my colleagues used to say, "AI is a mirror." I find that insightful: it reflects who you are, including the curiosity, judgment, and habits you bring to it. The questions you ask and the standards you apply to its answers matter. An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability, reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse. Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not? The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can make the instrument more useful. Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the person actually does. What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire." Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them "conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any. I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator has surrendered their judgment. The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

stories.title: Muse Spark Open
stories.author: bigwheels
summaryZh: Muse Spark Open is available today and brings leading agentic capabilities to your desktop for the first time on Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Today, we’re releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weight model to date. Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal model with 816B total parameters (42B active) and a 1M-token context window. Built for coding and agentic work, it excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning. We believe the future is for everyone, and that includes the freedom to run advanced models wherever, including at home. Muse Spark Open is the first model in its class to run on your desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with the latest MLX framework. Muse Spark Open is available today through API platforms at Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. Model weights are available for download on Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden, Hugging Face, and Microsoft Foundry Models. It runs on leading inference engines like SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, Apple MLX, llama.cpp, and Unsloth with optimizations for AMD, Apple, Intel, and NVIDIA silicon. Developers can easily further customize the model using the PyTorch framework.Key Benchmarks

For more details about our evaluations, see the evaluation methodology report. Optimized for Apple Silicon Leveraging the latest version of MLX, Muse Spark Open was optimized to run on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, and together they’re the best way to run a powerful model on your own desktop. Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra's integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory. We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically. Available Now We’re sharing this work because we want everyone to have access to the best models. The open-weight version of Muse Spark ships with custom, auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang, delivering 1.03-3.95× kernel-level speedups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350. Safety and Preparedness Releasing open-weight models is part of how we bring the benefits of personal superintelligence to everyone, and part of how safety work advances across the field. Open weights also carry their own considerations, and Muse Spark Open has additional safety post-training for that reason. The results demonstrate strong safeguards across risk categories measured. We evaluated the model in line with our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework, covering the most severe risks, and it met the thresholds our framework requires for release. Detailed results are in the Muse Spark Open model card, with a full evaluation report available soon. License We’re releasing the weights under the Muse Model License with limited commercial terms, which allow many developers to use the model for free. Get Started You can customize Muse Spark Open for your use case by leveraging PyTorch’s TorchTitan to further tune the model. To run it on Apple silicon, use MLX, which pulls the weights directly from Hugging Face. Muse Spark Open is available now through Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/collections/meta-models/muse-spark-open MLX Adapter for running Muse Spark Open on Mac Studio. Hosted Inference Partners: Together AI, Fireworks, Baseten, Modal, Groq, Nebius, and OpenRouter. Built or published something with Muse Spark Open? Share with us on the Hugging Face Forums — we’d love to see what you create.
